links.outcome: Policy robustness when evaluated under varied reward-function weightings (cross-OPE)
links.effect: Only 9,635 (56%) of 17,182 policies passing initial OPE passed cross-OPE; 44% showed suboptimal performance under alternate reward weightings, indicating overfitting or poor generalisability.
links.quote: Despite the successful performance of the models in the initial evaluation phase, a considerable number failed to exhibit comparable results during the cross-OPE evaluation utilising an alternate reward function shape.

links.outcome: Whether clinical policy inspection detects problems missed by quantitative off-policy evaluation
links.effect: A model with top-decile positive OPE and cross-OPE results showed bias against one action (PEEP 10–14, FiO2 80–100%), which could disqualify it from clinical implementation; OPE alone was insufficient.
links.quote: Although the policies show clinically reasonable action recommendations, the bias in this model could disqualify it from clinical implementation, highlighting that OPE results alone are insufficient for a robust model and policy evaluation.

links.effect: Restricted policy limited recommendations to less aggressive choices, barring potentially optimal but riskier actions; no rate reported.
links.quote: Inherent to our safety-restricted policy design, clinical decisions can be more optimal than the RL-derived policy, as the safety-restricted policy limits the selection to less aggressive choices, barring potentially optimal but riskier actions.
